title: On the Automatability of Tree-Like k-DNF Resolution
abstract: A proof system 𝒫 is said to be automatable in time f(N) if there exists an algorithm that given as input an unsatisfiable formula F outputs a refutation of F in the proof system 𝒫 in time f(N), where N is the size of the smallest 𝒫-refutation of F plus the size of F. Atserias and Bonet (ECCC 2002), observed that tree-like k-DNF resolution is automatable in time N^{c⋅klog N} for a universal constant c. We show that, under the randomized exponential-time hypothesis (rETH), this is tight up to a O(log k)-factor in the exponent, i.e., we prove that tree-like k-DNF resolution, for k at most logarithmic in the number of variables of F, is not automatable in time N^o((k/log k)⋅log N) unless rETH is false. Our proof builds on the non-automatability results for resolution by Atserias and Müller (FOCS 2019), for algebraic proof systems by de Rezende, Göös, Nordström, Pitassi, Robere and Sokolov (STOC 2021), and for tree-like resolution by de Rezende (LAGOS 2021).

      Abstract
A proof system P is said to be automatable in time f (N ) if there exists an algorithm that given
as input an unsatisfiable formula F outputs a refutation of F in the proof system P in time f (N ),
where N is the size of the smallest P-refutation of F plus the size of F . Atserias and Bonet (ECCC
2002), observed that tree-like k-DNF resolution is automatable in time N c·k log N for a universal
constant c. We show that, under the randomized exponential-time hypothesis (rETH), this is tight
up to a O(log k)-factor in the exponent, i.e., we prove that tree-like k-DNF resolution, for k at most
logarithmic in the number of variables of F , is not automatable in time N o((k/ log k)·log N ) unless
rETH is false. Our proof builds on the non-automatability results for resolution by Atserias and
Müller (FOCS 2019), for algebraic proof systems by de Rezende, Göös, Nordström, Pitassi, Robere
and Sokolov (STOC 2021), and for tree-like resolution by de Rezende (LAGOS 2021).

 1      Introduction
A central question in proof complexity concerns the difficulty of finding proofs: given a
theorem, can we efficiently find a proof of it in a given proof system? This question – whether
proof search is automatable – was first raised informally by Gödel in a 1956 letter to von
Neumann [39] and has been studied formally since the 1990s when Bonet, Pitassi and Raz
introduced the notion of automatability. A proof system P is said to be automatable in
time f (N ) if there exists an algorithm that, given an unsatisfiable formula F , outputs a
refutation of F in P in time f (N ), where N denotes the sum of the size of the smallest
P-refutation of F and the size of F .
    A series of results in the late 1990s and early 2000s established non-automatability of
various proof systems under standard complexity-theoretic and cryptographic assumptions
[7, 26, 28, 12, 1, 11, 5, 2, 21]. While cryptographic assumptions remain the only known way
to proving non-automatability of Frege systems beyond AC 0 -Frege [3], recent years have
seen renewed interest in understanding the automatability of weaker systems [31, 6, 23, 22,

           A key frontier in this line of research involves understanding the automatability of tree-
       like proof systems. These systems correspond to natural search algorithms that explore the
       solution space via branching heuristics. Thus, non-automatability results for such systems
       translate into lower bounds for SAT solvers implementing these heuristics. A canonical
       example is tree-like resolution, where derived clauses may only be used once to derive
       new clauses. Robinson [37] showed that tree-like resolution is polynomially equivalent to
       non-deterministic DPLL [15, 14] algorithms.
           The DPLL algorithm searches for satisfying assignments to a CNF formula F by recursively
       branching on the assignment of a variable. A natural generalization of this algorithm is to
       allows branching on Boolean functions that depend only on a small number of variables.
       Such algorithms correspond to the tree-like k-DNF resolution proof system (Res(k)), a
       generalization of tree-like resolution where up to k literals may be resolved at once.
           Automating tree-like proof systems involves efficiently identifying good branching choices.
       This is often challenging, and many tree-like proof systems are not known to be automatable
       even in random subexponential time. The exceptions, for which non-trivial automating
       algorithms are known, are tree-like resolution and tree-like k-DNF resolution: Beame and
       Pitassi [7] proposed a simple automating algorithm for tree-like resolution running in time
       N O(log N ) , which was later adapted by Atserias and Bonet [4] to show that tree-like k-DNF
       resolution is automatable in time N c·k log N , for a universal constant c, independent of k.
       This latter result holds even when k is a function of the number of variables of the formula,

       procedure from [20], implies that if tree-like resolution is automatable in polynomial time,
       then W[P] = FPT. More recently, Mertz, Pitassi and Wei [31] proved that automating

       1.1    Our result
       We prove our result under the randomized exponential time hypothesis which we introduce
       next. The exponential time hypothesis (ETH), is the strengthening of the P ̸= NP conjecture,
       introduced by Impagliazzo and Paturi [24], that states that 3-SAT cannot be solved in
       subexponential time. More formally, it states that there exists an ε > 0 such that 3-SAT for
       n-variate formulas cannot be decided in deterministic time 2εn . The randomized exponential
       time hypothesis (rETH), introduced by Dell et al. [19], is instead a strengthening of the
       NP ̸⊆ BPP conjecture. It asserts that there exists ε > 0 and c > 1 such that 3-SAT for
       n-variate formulas with cn clauses cannot be decided in randomized time 2εn .

a natural way, that F has a (DAG-like) resolution refutation of size at most s. The idea

       1.3      Our technical contribution
       In most of the follow-up works to [6], the main technical challenge was to show that, when F
       is unsatisfiable, there exist no small refutations of A(F ) for some proof system P, which
       was typically stronger than resolution. For tree-like resolution, however, the main difficulty
       is quite different. Pudlák’s upper bound [34] for the case where F satisfiable is inherently
       DAG-like, and the best known tree-like resolution refutations are of exponential size. In
       fact, we do not expect significantly smaller tree-like resolution refutations of Ref(F, s) to
       exist. In particular, if there were such refutations of polynomial size, then the algorithm
       of [7] that automates tree-like resolution in quasi-polynomial time would imply that NP is in
       quasi-polynomial time. Overcoming this limitation requires a substantial modification to the
       structure of A(F ).

 2     Preliminaries and proof overview
In this section we state Theorem 1 formally and show why it follows from Theorem 2. We
then present the idea behind the construction of the formula output by the algorithm A of
Theorem 2. Before starting, we need to introduce some notation and definitions.
    For a positive integer n, the set {1, . . . , n} is denoted by [n]. Given a Boolean variable x
ranging over {0, 1}, its positive literal is x (sometimes denoted as x1 ) and its negative literal
is x (sometimes denoted as x0 ). A clause is a disjunction of literals ℓ1 ∨ · · · ∨ ℓt and a term
is a conjunction of literals ℓ1 ∧ · · · ∧ ℓt . We view clauses and terms as sets: the order of the
literals is irrelevant, and we can assume there are no repetitions.
    A CNF formula {C1 , . . . , Cm } is a conjunction of clauses C1 ∧ · · · ∧ Cm and a DNF
formula is a disjunction of terms T1 ∨ · · · ∨ Tm . A k-CNF formula is a CNF formula where
every clause has at most k literals and analogously a k-DNF formula is a DNF formula where
every term has at most k literals. We say that a variable x appears in a clause C or in a
term T if a literal over x is an element of C or of T , respectively. A formula is satisfiable if
there exists an assignment to the Boolean variables of the formula that sets its value to 1;
otherwise it is said to be unsatisfiable.
    The k-DNF resolution proof system, denoted by Res(k), is a proof system where each
lines is a k-DNFs and new lines can be derived from previous one using any of the following

2.3    Intuition for construction of A(F )
Let F be a CNF formula over variables x1 , . . . , xn with poly(n) clauses. The Ref(F, s)
formula encodes that there is a resolution refutation of F of size s, which is usually chosen to
be a polynomial in n. As mentioned earlier, Pudlák’s [34] upper bound for Ref(F, s) when F
is satisfiable, which was adapted in [6], is intrinsically DAG-like. We do not expect there
to be polynomial-size tree-like Res(k) refutations of Ref(F, s) for satisfiable F since, due to
the quasi-polynomial algorithm that automates tree-like Res(k), this would imply that it
is possible to solve SAT in quasi-polynomial time. It may be the case that tree-like Res(k)
requires size at least 2Ω(n) to refute Ref(F, s), regardless of whether F is satisfiable and,
therefore, it seems that non-automatability results for tree-like Res(k) are unlikely to be
obtained using this formula.
    In order to describe the formula ShortcutRef k (F ) we first describe a simplified version of
ShortcutRef 1 (F ), which is inspired by the formula ShallowRef(F ) from [16]. Consider the
trivial tree-like resolution refutation of a formula F , denoted by Π, corresponding to the
refutation of depth n that has 2n leaves, one for every width-n clause (each of which is a
weakening of some axiom), and that resolves over variables in reverse order, that is, xn then
xn−1 , etc., until it resolves over x1 to derive the empty clause. We view the clauses of this
refutation as arranged in layers, and we say that all clauses that are obtained by resolving
over variable i are in layer i.
    We can create a formula stating that this tree-like resolution refutation fits into a smaller
structure as follows (see Figure 1). The variables of this formula are partitioned into blocks,
one block for each clause of the purported structured derivation. The structure of the blocks
is as follows. We start from the top of the refutation (the part closest to ⊥) and for the first
2q layers we simply copy the first 2q layers of Π (i.e., copy the structure and the clauses). At
this point, we have 22q leaves and our structure is starting to get too big. We therefore create
a new layer with only 2q blocks and encode (the contradictory statement) that, actually,
the 22q blocks of the layer above can be mapped in a one-to-one fashion to these 2q new
blocks. This mapping is encoded by enforcing that if block B is mapped to block B ′ then
both contain the exact same clause. Starting from each of the 2q new blocks, we construct a
full binary tree of blocks of depth q. This gives us 22q blocks at the last layer and we again
map these blocks to 2q blocks. By repeating this procedure n/q times, we create a structure
of depth n, but that has size only 2O(q) . For reasons that will become clear soon, we encode
the mapping from 22q to 2q as a pigeonhole principle instance over an expander of constant
degree ∆. Note that this structure has size 2O(q) .

 6     Concluding remarks
                                                                                      k
In this work, we prove that automating tree-like k-DNF resolution in time no( log k ·log n) is
rETH-hard. This implies that, assuming rETH, the automating algorithm proposed by
Atserias and Bonet [4] is optimal up to an O(log k) in the exponent. A natural open problem
is whether a similar result can be obtained under ETH. If we maintain the overall structure of
our argument, obtaining the derandomization would be equivalent to designing a deterministic
poly-time algorithm able to construct constant-degree polynomially unbalanced expander
graphs. This question has been extensively studied in the area of pseudorandomness and
remains an outstanding open problem. It worth mentioning that, for our application, we
are allowed to relax the condition classically imposed on the size of the sets of vertices that
expand, and in particular we may assume it to be polylogarithmic in the number of vertices.
    Numerous intriguing unresolved problems involve automatability. We just focus on some
of the ones most relevant to this work. As mentioned in the introduction, one of the frontiers
of automatability results lies in understanding tree-like proof systems. It is highly plausible
that the vast majority of tree-like proof systems are as hard to automate as their DAG-like
counterparts. Nevertheless, many (weak) tree-like proof systems are unable to establish the
upper bound needed to prove non-automatability results by the now standard techniques.
Can we bypass this obstacle for concrete proof systems such as tree-like Res(⊕) (resolution
over linear equations mod 2) or tree-like cutting planes and obtain a non-automatability
result which is stronger than what we know for tree-like resolution?
    Very few non-trivial automating algorithm are known when automatability is defined
with respect to size. However, there exist alternative definitions for automatability where the
size parameter is substituted, for example, by degree or width, and in those cases there are
some automating algorithms [13, 9, 32, 35]. Are these algorithms optimal? Partial results
can be derived from [6].
